justification: None of the listed articles reports any human genetic variant in KCNC1 associated with epilepsy or seizures; the only human mutation screening (in Usher syndrome type IC families, PMIDs 9041816, 9445488) excluded KCNC1 coding mutations and concerns deafness, not epilepsy. The remaining literature is biophysical/expression work on Kv3.1 channels in heterologous systems, rodent and avian brain, and knockout mice (PMIDs 11877504, 10531438, 12592408), showing a role in fast-spiking GABAergic interneuron and reticular thalamic firing — biology plausibly relevant to cortical/thalamic excitability and thus epileptogenesis, but epilepsy is never measured or mentioned. This supports at most a hypothesized, mechanism-based relationship rather than any genetic association. Because the epilepsy phenotype is entirely absent from these abstracts, a substantial probability also remains that, on this evidence alone, the relationship should be called novel. Established and Existing are essentially excluded since no human probands or families with KCNC1 variants and seizures are reported.

justification: The only human autism-relevant article is a single case report of an autistic boy with a large de novo interstitial 4q32–q34 deletion (~19 Mb, 33 genes) rendering him hemizygous for GRIA2/AMPA2 along with GLRA3, GLRB, NPY1R and NPY5R (PMID 15090072); the authors explicitly state that further studies are needed to confirm involvement. Because this is a multigene copy-number change in one proband, it cannot single out GRIA2 and therefore cannot support "Established", though it provides a limited, human-based candidate-gene suggestion bordering on "Existing". All other listed papers concern GRIA2/GluR2 biology unrelated to autism — RNA editing, AMPA receptor structure and allosteric modulation, motoneuron disease/ALS, SCA1, gliomas, and rodent/in vitro models (PMIDs 11717408, 15827116, 12015593, 16192394, 9178165) — which at most support a hypothesized mechanistic link via synaptic glutamatergic plasticity. Hence the evidence is split between a weak human association (Existing) and purely biological plausibility (Hypothesized), with Established effectively excluded and Novel unlikely given the explicit candidate-gene proposal.

justification: None of the three articles concerns epilepsy or seizures in any form. CHRNA1 here is described exclusively as the muscle-specific nicotinic acetylcholine receptor alpha-subunit, with evidence tied to neuromuscular junction biology: a zebrafish gain-of-function mutation modeling slow-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome (PMID 15128655), zebrafish muscle fibre formation via acetylcholine/calcium signalling (PMID 16249237), and CHRNA1 as the autoantigen in myasthenia gravis (PMID 12935778). No human genetic variant, association study, or even mechanistic pathway linking CHRNA1 to seizure susceptibility is presented, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A small amount of probability is retained for Hypothesized only because cholinergic receptor subunits and calcium-mediated excitability are broadly relevant to neuronal hyperexcitability, but these data are muscle-specific and in non-human models.
